title: A tiny excess of one mirror-image molecule can grow until it takes over the whole flask
body: On 7 October 2026 Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing how one mirror-image form of a molecule can win out. Many molecules come in a left- and a right-handed form, and life uses only one: the amino acids in proteins are left-handed, the sugars in DNA right-handed. Ordinary reactions make both equally. In 1986 Kagan found that a catalyst only partly one-handed can give a product more one-handed than itself, because its chiral parts pair up and the mixed left–right pairs barely work. Soai then found a molecule that catalyses its own formation: a lead of 0.00005% for one hand grew to over 99.5% in three runs, and when he started with no lead at all, chance chose the winner. His reaction is not life’s chemistry, but it shows how a tiny imbalance can turn into one hand, as the [Nobel committee’s background](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/popular-chemistryprize2026-2.pdf) explains.

slides.question: A catalyst is 75% right-handed and 25% left. In Kagan’s example, how right-handed does the reaction behave?
slides.explanation: Like 90%. Its chiral parts pair at random: 56% right–right, 38% mixed, 6% left–left. The mixed pairs barely work, so the reaction runs on 56 parts right to 6 parts left.

slides.alt: Animation on ivory paper with a silver mirror line: a rose left hand and a teal right hand, then a molecule that never matches its mirror image. Flasks of rose and teal dots go from 50:50 to one-sided; Kagan's 75% catalyst pairs up and acts like 90%; Soai's runs climb to over 99.5%.

slides.prompt: Run rounds from a slight right-handed lead. How many until one hand passes 99%?
slides.takeaway: From 50.5% it takes 8 rounds: while the lead is small it doubles each round, because mixed pairs drop out. Let mixed pairs work too and nothing changes: holding back the other hand is what lets one hand win.

slides.heading: Soai’s reaction: how far one hand leads, in %
slides.note: Lead = right minus left, as a share of all. Run 3: over 99.5%.

slides.heading: Why drug makers care
slides.text: Many drug molecules come in two mirror forms. Often one has the effect you want, while the other does nothing or causes side effects, so chemists try to make only the useful one. Kagan’s non-linear effects are now a standard tool for designing such reactions, and for working out how they happen.

slides.question: What did Soai’s 2003 reaction start from?
slides.explanation: It started from molecules with no handedness. By chance a little more of one form appeared, and that form took over. Run again, the other hand could win instead.
